# Auction Playbook

When I see a lot's value to me and the current standing bid, I calculate the profit margin (value minus bid) to guide my decision.

When a lot is worth significantly more to me than the current bid, I bid to win it. The profit margin matters more than the absolute price.

When I bid, I use the minimum raise only if it still leaves me substantial profit. I don't bid conservatively just because a minimum raise is available.

When I'm in round 1 of 2, I reserve budget for remaining lots rather than depleting my funds early. I track how many lots remain and keep dry powder.

When the standing bid is very low relative to the lot's value to me, I bid aggressively because the value extraction is high even after multiple raises.

When a lot is worth less to me than the estimate suggests it's worth generally, I'm cautious about bidding wars. I don't chase lots where my private value is below market signal. Passing preserves budget for lots where my valuation better aligns with market signals.

When I win a lot at a good price, I recognize this as success and use it as a baseline for evaluating future lots.

When it's the final lot and no more opportunities remain, I bid what the lot is worth to me minus what I can still afford to pay profitably. I don't hold back dry powder that won't be used.

I track which bidders are winning which lots and by how much. This shows me whether I'm competitive and helps me identify which lots I should prioritize fighting for.

I must track my budget accurately throughout the game. The budget I state in each reply must reflect actual cumulative spending so far. If I've spent 24 total across all lots won, I have 6 left—not a placeholder figure. Accurate budget tracking is essential for correct decision-making in later rounds and is non-negotiable.

When standing bid is low relative to my valuation and it's round 2 (the final round for that lot), I should bid to win because no further opportunity exists. This is different from round 1, where I might pass to reserve budget.

I should open at a competitive level in round 1 when no bids exist yet. Opening at 4 on a lot worth 34 is reasonable value-setting that establishes my presence without over-committing.

I will not bid on a lot worth less to me than the standing bid, even if profit is possible. In lot 4, I bid 6 when the lot was worth only 16—I should have passed. Negative or razor-thin margins are not worth my remaining budget when other opportunities may exist.

I will be disciplined about budget exhaustion. Once my budget is depleted or nearly depleted, I cannot bid on remaining lots. I must make spending decisions early that preserve optionality for later lots, especially high-value ones that might appear in round 2.

When I'm down to very low remaining budget (under 10), I should bid only on lots where my value significantly exceeds the standing bid, and only if it's round 2 (final chance). In round 1 with low budget, I should pass to preserve capital.

# Auction Playbook

When I see a lot where my valuation significantly exceeds the current standing bid, I bid the minimum raise to take control and secure value.

When I see a lot where my valuation is below the estimate and notably below the current bid trajectory, I pass immediately to preserve budget for better opportunities.

When multiple bidders remain and a lot reaches my valuation, I continue bidding rather than passing, since the competition will likely drive the price higher if I step out.

When I'm in the final round of a lot and the current bid is well below my valuation, I bid to win rather than conserve—there's no future opportunity cost to winning value at that point.

I track my cumulative spending against my budget to know what runway I have for remaining lots. After each lot, I recalculate my remaining budget and adjust my bidding aggressiveness accordingly.

I pay attention to what other bidders win and at what price—this tells me about their valuations and their aggression level, which informs how high I expect prices to go on future lots.

When deciding whether to bid, I compare the current bid against my own valuation, not against the estimate. The estimate is just context for the market; my private value is what matters for my profit.

I do not bid on lots where my valuation is close to or below the estimate, especially early in an auction when I have limited information about other bidders' patterns. Wait for clearer value opportunities.

When I pass in an early round, I should have a strong reason (low valuation relative to estimate or current bid), not just caution. Passing too much costs me opportunities.

**I must verify my budget calculations before every bid.** My budget tracking failed badly this episode—I lost track of actual spending and thought I had far more runway than I did. I will manually subtract each bid amount from my remaining budget and write down the result before replying. When the system displays budget, I treat it as my baseline check, but I independently verify the arithmetic.

**When my valuation is very close to the estimate (within 1–2 points), I treat that as a red flag.** It signals the market values the lot higher than I do. On lot 5, my value was 28 and the estimate was 27—barely a margin. I should have passed or bid only if the standing bid was extremely low (say, 2 or less). The minimal edge is not worth competing for.

**I must clarify whether I am winning at the standing bid or at my own bid amount.** If the standing bid is 6 and I raise to 9, I win at 9, not at 6. This means my profit is value minus my bid, not value minus the standing bid. Before bidding, I calculate: will I profit if I win at my bid amount, or only if I win at the standing bid?

**I bid more aggressively on lots where my valuation clearly exceeds the estimate,** especially early in the auction when I have full budget. These are genuine edges. Lot 1 (value 52, estimate 34) was a clear win at 16. I should have bid more boldly to lock in control early.

**I do not pass in round 1 expecting to re-engage in round 2.** Passing in round 1 often means I lose the lot entirely if other bidders compete in round 2. If my valuation is above the opening bid or estimate, I should bid in round 1 to secure optionality. Lot 2 exemplified this: I passed in round 1 and lost the option to bid in round 2.

**I budget conservatively for later lots.** After each win, I immediately recalculate how much budget I've spent and how many lots remain. On lot 4, I had only 10 left after spending 20 on lot 3. With 2 lots remaining, I should not have spent 8 of that 10. I should have passed lot 4 and preserved runway for lot 5.

**When I'm in the final lot with constrained budget, I bid only if the value is clear and the standing bid is very low.** On lot 5, I had only 10 left. The lot was worth 28 (barely above estimate 27), the standing bid was 0, but I knew I might face bidding wars. Bidding 9 of my final 10 left me with almost no negotiating room. I should have passed lot 5 or been willing to walk away if the price moved above 5–6.

**I treat the standing bid as a signal of other bidders' interest.** When a standing bid jumps significantly from round 1 to round 2 (lot 4: 0 to 6, lot 5: 3 to 6), it means another bidder entered or raised. I should not assume I can win at the minimum raise; I may face escalation.

**I win or lose on margins.** My final score was +14. That came from winning lot 3 at 20 (value 35, profit 15), despite losses on lot 5 (value 28, paid 9, profit 19—wait, that's a win). Let me recalculate: lot 3 won at 20 with value 35 = +15. Lot 5 won at 9 with value 28 = +19. But my score is +14, so I must have had a losing lot. Lot 1 was a loss: stood at 7 in round 1, but the system shows lot 1 won by bidder 2 at 19. I did not win lot 1 after bidding 7 and 16. That means I was outbid and lost the money, or the scoring is different than I thought. I should clarify the scoring system: do I lose the full bid amount if I'm outbid, or only pay if I win? Assuming I pay only if I win, I must have won only lots 3 and 5, and lot 1 went to bidder 2. That reconciles to 35 - 20 + 28 - 9 = 34, not 14. I am missing something about the scoring or the episode results. Regardless, I should focus on winning high-margin lots and passing low-margin or uncertain lots.

# Playbook for Ref Auction

**On valuation and bidding basics:**
When a lot's value to me exceeds the standing bid by a significant margin, I bid to take control rather than pass. The gap between estimate and true value is my information advantage—use it.

When no one has bid yet, open at minimum to gather information cheaply and establish position without waste.

When I'm in a strong position on a lot (high value, low bid), bid the minimum raise to preserve budget while staying competitive. Don't jump aggressively when you don't need to.

**On budget management:**
Track my remaining budget carefully after each winning bid. In this episode I finished with 64 remaining after spending only 36 on three winning lots—this is still significant waste, though better than before.

My wins (lot 1 at 19, lot 4 at 8, lot 5 at 9) scored +79 total. But I passed on lot 2 round 2 and lot 3 round 2 due to insufficient margins or competitive pressure. With budget remaining, I should have competed harder on at least one of these.

Commit budget more aggressively on high-confidence lots earlier in the game. Don't let competitive loss on one lot (lot 2) cause me to retreat and under-deploy on subsequent lots.

**On competitive dynamics:**
When another bidder wins a lot early, don't assume I've lost my opportunity to win overall. Lot 2 went to bidder 0 at 16; I passed round 2. This was the right call—value 52 vs. bid 16 left only 36 points, but the standing bid had already doubled from 8 to 16 in one round, signaling strong competition. Passing was correct.

On lot 3, I passed round 2 entirely. This was a retreat I shouldn't make. If I value a lot positively against the standing bid, I should bid.

Track total wins, not just total budget spent. I won 3 of 5 lots—a strong competitive position. The remaining 64 budget suggests I could have pushed for a fourth if value aligned.

**On valuation edge and discipline:**
Only bid when value to me exceeds the standing bid by a meaningful margin. A small or eroding margin is a signal to exit.

On lot 1 round 2: value 44 vs. bid 16 left 28 points—strong edge, bid decisively. Correct.

On lot 4 round 2: value 26 vs. bid 6 left 20 points—clear edge, bid to control. Correct.

On lot 5 rounds 1 and 2: value 45 vs. opening bid 3, then vs. my own bid 6, left substantial margins both times. Winning at 9 was very profitable. Correct.

On lot 2 round 2: value 52 vs. standing bid 8, minimum raise to 12 would leave 40 points. This is a large edge—I should have bid here. I passed, which was an error. The bid had jumped from my 4 to someone else's 8 in round 1, but that's not a reason to abandon a 40-point edge.

**On knowing when to stop:**
Passing is correct only when value edge is gone or when I've run out of budget. In this episode I had budget available and passed on lot 2 round 2 due to the standing bid jump. That was emotional, not logical. If I value the lot at 52 and standing bid is 8-12, I should bid.

Lot 3: I didn't see the full details, but I passed entirely. If I had positive value edge, I should have bid at least once.

**On knowing when to bid harder:**
Minimum raises preserve budget but can signal weakness or indecision to other bidders. When I have a large value edge and want to secure a lot, a slightly larger raise (not minimum) can discourage competition without waste—e.g., raising to 10 instead of 8 on a 6-standing bid.

I executed this well on lot 1 round 1 (bid 10 on 7 standing) and overall played conservative but effective raises.

**On scoring discipline:**
My final score of +79 came from three winning lots with strong value edges. This beat my previous game (which yielded +14) by a large margin.

The key difference was competing more actively on multiple lots rather than retreating after early losses. I won 3 of 5 and scored well. Next time, apply this same confidence to lots 2 and 3: if I have value, I bid.

Seek positive spread opportunities and bid to capture them. High value + low bid = winning bid. Don't abandon that logic when a standing bid moves up in a single round—the absolute spread is what matters, not the trajectory.

**On round 2 psychology:**
In round 2 of any lot, I'm seeing the final opportunity to secure it. If I value it positively and have budget, I should be more inclined to bid decisively, not less. Lot 2 round 2 was the critical miss: I should have bid there.

Reserve passing for true cases where margin has collapsed or budget is exhausted, not for lots where I've simply lost the first round.
